name: Independent on Sunday cryptic crossword No 1,664

clue.text: Hit hard — huge anticlimax

blocks.note: to bat is to hit, as with a cricket bat
H is the pencil abbreviation for hard
OS is short for outsize, a clothing label for very large sizes

explanation.surface: A heavy blow lands, followed by a big letdown.
explanation.walkthrough: The dash makes it read as one dramatic event, but the first three words are wordplay; OS (outsize) is a standard crossword abbreviation for huge.
explanation.definitionFit: Bathos is a sudden ludicrous drop from the lofty to the trivial, which is precisely what a literary letdown amounts to.

clue.text: Character seen with drink — John Lennon for one

blocks.note: an air is a manner or demeanour, a person's character
port is a fortified wine

explanation.surface: A Beatle depicted alongside a glass of something.
explanation.walkthrough: John Lennon looks like a person to be defined, but Liverpool's airport is named Liverpool John Lennon Airport.
explanation.definitionFit: Liverpool's main air terminal was renamed in honour of the Beatle, so his name labels one example of the category.

clue.text: Manage large snake accommodated in sweltering mobile home

indicators.note: to be accommodated somewhere is to be housed inside it, so one piece sits within another

blocks.note: sweltering weather is very hot
to use something is to manage or handle it
a boa is a large constricting snake

explanation.surface: Someone coping with a big snake in a stifling caravan.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Mobile home' suggests a caravan, which fits the sweltering scene, but a home that floats is also mobile.
explanation.definitionFit: A boat fitted out as living quarters is a dwelling that can travel, a home that moves on water.

clue.text: Extremely sensitive judoka provides chair

indicators.note: the extremes of a word are its two ends, so only the outermost letters are kept

blocks.note: first and last letters of the word
a dan is a black-belt grade in judo, so a judoka may be one

explanation.surface: A very touchy martial artist supplies a seat.
explanation.walkthrough: A dan is a grade of black belt, and by extension the person holding it.
explanation.definitionFit: A sedan chair is an enclosed seat carried on poles, so sedan alone can stand for that portable seat.

clue.text: Infatuation as fellow gathers everyone round female

indicators.note: to gather is to take in and enclose, so one piece holds the rest
going round something means surrounding it, so the outer piece wraps the inner

blocks.note: cove is old slang for a chap or fellow
everyone is all
F is the abbreviation for female

explanation.surface: A man gathers everyone around a woman he is smitten with.
explanation.walkthrough: Cove is a dated British slang word for a man; two nested enclosures build the answer from the inside out.
explanation.definitionFit: Calf love is the idiom for a youthful crush, a passing romantic obsession felt by adolescents.

clue.text: Make merry in saloon on river?

blocks.note: a saloon is a type of car (a sedan in American English)
the Ouse is an English river

explanation.surface: Revelling in a riverboat bar.
explanation.walkthrough: Saloon suggests a bar, but here it is the British word for a family car; 'on' places it above the river in a down entry.
explanation.definitionFit: To carouse is to drink and revel noisily, the boisterous partying the phrase describes.

clue.text: Wild demon possibly displaying crude character

indicators.note: possibly signals one of several arrangements, so these letters may be rearranged

blocks.note: the letters of both words used as fodder

explanation.surface: A savage fiend showing a coarse nature.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Wild' looks like the anagram signal but is part of the fodder; 'possibly' is the signal.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone vulgar and base in their thinking shows coarse tastes, which is a sign of a crude nature.

clue.text: Truck coming from Ayr rolled over

indicators.note: coming from means taken out of, so the letters sit inside the words that follow
turning over flips the order, so the letters run backwards

blocks.note: letters spanning the two words, read before turning

explanation.surface: A truck overturned on its way from a Scottish town.
explanation.walkthrough: Ayr is a town on Scotland's west coast; 'rolled over' looks like one phrase but 'rolled' is part of the hiding place.
explanation.definitionFit: Lorry is the standard British word for a heavy goods vehicle, what Americans call a truck.

clue.text: He composed line put in exam papers for sending back

indicators.note: putting something in places it inside, so one piece goes between the others
sending something back returns it the way it came, so its letters run backwards

blocks.note: a viva is an oral examination
L is the abbreviation for line
ID is identity papers

explanation.surface: A setter slips a line into exam scripts before returning them.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Exam papers' reads as one phrase but splits into two pieces; a viva is the oral defence of a thesis in British universities.
explanation.definitionFit: Antonio Vivaldi was a Venetian Baroque composer famous for The Four Seasons, so he is a man who composed.

clue.text: 2 team expanded to restrict heat and carbon

indicators.note: to restrict something is to hem it in, so one piece encloses the others

blocks.note: something that expanded grew
a heat is a preliminary round of a competition
C is the chemical symbol for carbon

explanation.surface: A team grows bigger in order to control heating and carbon emissions.
explanation.walkthrough: The 2 refers to the answer at 2 Down, AIRPORT; 'heat' sounds like temperature but is a qualifying contest.
explanation.definitionFit: The staff who service and refuel aircraft between flights at an aerodrome are its ground staff, a team working at an airport.

clue.text: Wander across where the last shall be first

indicators.text: where the last shall be first
indicators.note: the biblical phrase describes the final item moving to the front, so the end letter moves to the start

blocks.note: to go across is to go over

explanation.surface: Roaming about in a place where the biblical order is turned upside down.
explanation.walkthrough: The phrase comes from the Gospel saying 'the last shall be first'; here it moves the final R of OVER to the front.
explanation.definitionFit: To rove is to roam or travel about without a fixed destination, a direct synonym of the verb given.

clue.text: Single month — November or August?

blocks.note: sole means single or only
M is the abbreviation for month
N is November in the NATO phonetic alphabet

explanation.surface: Asking which single month is meant: November or August?
explanation.walkthrough: August looks like another month to match November, but the capital disguises the adjective august, meaning stately.
explanation.definitionFit: The adjective august describes something dignified and impressive, which shares meaning with grave, serious and stately.

clue.text: One going round on this bike?

blocks.note: uni- is the prefix meaning one
a cycle is a going round, a revolution

explanation.surface: A rider circling on a particular bicycle.
explanation.walkthrough: It reads as a description of someone riding laps, but 'one' and 'going round' build the word, and the question mark flags the play.
explanation.definitionFit: A cycle with a single wheel is still loosely a bike, a pedalled machine ridden for transport or show.

clue.text: Name for German unchanged by revolution

indicators.note: a word that survives being turned right round reads the same in both directions

blocks.note: a typical German man's forename, chosen because it reads the same both ways

explanation.surface: A German name that survived a political uprising.
explanation.walkthrough: Revolution suggests politics in Germany, but it means turning the word round end to end.
explanation.definitionFit: Otto is a traditional male forename, borne by Bismarck and several Holy Roman emperors.

clue.text: Fine results in going beyond this potentially simple diet

definitions.text: Fine results in going beyond this

indicators.note: potentially means what something could become, so these letters could become another arrangement

blocks.note: the letters of both words used as fodder

explanation.surface: Good outcomes might come from going beyond a basic eating plan.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fine' reads as an adjective praising results, but here it is a penalty paid by a motorist.
explanation.definitionFit: Exceeding the legal maximum velocity on a road gets a driver a monetary penalty, so this is what you go beyond.

clue.text: Plan to have precious stone beneath rock layers

indicators.note: in a down entry, a part that lies beneath another is written after it

blocks.note: strata are layers of rock
a gem is a precious stone

explanation.surface: A scheme to find a jewel buried under the rock beds.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down entry, 'beneath' puts GEM below STRATA.
explanation.definitionFit: A stratagem is a cunning scheme or ploy devised to outwit someone, a crafty kind of scheme.

clue.text: Force endlessly hurt when called into question

indicators.note: without an end, the word loses its final letter

blocks.note: impel means force, here cut short
something that hurt ached

explanation.surface: Constant pain from being challenged by an inquiry.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Force' needs a verb form, impel, before its last letter goes.
explanation.definitionFit: To impeach can mean to challenge or cast doubt on someone's honesty or a witness's reliability, besides formally charging an official.

clue.text: Show with questions flower maiden keeps in memory

blocks.note: M is a maiden over in cricket scoring
an aster is a daisy-like flower
to keep something in mind is to keep it in memory

explanation.surface: A young woman holds a flower in her memory while watching a quiz.
explanation.walkthrough: Mastermind is a long-running BBC quiz show with a famous black chair; M for maiden comes from cricket scorecards.
explanation.definitionFit: The BBC television programme consists of contestants answering rounds of general knowledge and specialist subject queries.

clue.text: Gangster and nutter — one put out diary

indicators.note: to put out is to eject, so a letter is removed

blocks.note: Al Capone, the archetypal gangster
a nutter is a maniac, with I (one) removed

explanation.surface: A mobster and a madman, one of them tossing a journal aside.
explanation.walkthrough: Al Capone stands for any gangster in crosswords; MANIAC drops its I, the Roman numeral one.
explanation.definitionFit: An almanac is a yearly calendar of dates and events, so it serves the same purpose as a yearbook or diary.

clue.text: Jones for one cool with divine huntress

blocks.note: in means fashionable or cool
Diana is the Roman goddess of the hunt

explanation.surface: A man named Jones, calm beside a goddess of the chase.
explanation.walkthrough: Jones looks like the surname to define, but the answer is the first name of the film archaeologist Indiana Jones.
explanation.definitionFit: Indiana is the forename of Indiana Jones, so a Jones in the films is one example of someone so named.

clue.text: Huntsman has to go by lake

blocks.note: to go, informally, is to urinate
L is the abbreviation for lake

explanation.surface: A hunter needing a toilet stop near a lake.
explanation.walkthrough: John Peel was a Cumbrian huntsman celebrated in the folk song 'D'ye ken John Peel'.
explanation.definitionFit: The famous Lake District fox hunter of the old song makes this surname a proper-name example of a hunting man.

clue.text: Flat-bottomed vessels in Devon river region

indicators.note: being in something means sitting inside it, so one piece goes within the other

blocks.note: the Exe flows through Devon to Exeter
pans are flat-bottomed cooking vessels

explanation.surface: Punts or barges on a river in the west of England.
explanation.walkthrough: Flat-bottomed vessels sound like boats, which fits the river, but they are kitchen pans; Devon is a county in south-west England.
explanation.definitionFit: An expanse is a wide open area of land, sea or sky, a broad tract or stretch of territory.

clue.text: Brought in from anchorage in one sea

indicators.note: being in something means sitting inside it, so one piece is enclosed

blocks.note: I is the Roman numeral one
the Med is the Mediterranean Sea
a port is a harbour or anchorage

explanation.surface: Goods shipped in from a harbour on the same sea.
explanation.walkthrough: The Med is the everyday British shortening of the Mediterranean.
explanation.definitionFit: Goods that are imported have been carried into a country from abroad, a past participle for introducing from outside.

clue.text: Four pairs in old court given notice

blocks.note: O is the abbreviation for old
CT is the abbreviation for court
an ad is a notice, an advertisement

explanation.surface: Four couples in an ancient courtroom served with a notice.
explanation.walkthrough: Four pairs looks like people in a tennis court, but it is just the number eight.
explanation.definitionFit: An octad is a group or set of eight, and two times four makes eight items.

clue.text: Have mine where there's no time for seafood

indicators.note: saying there is no time means the time abbreviation is taken away

blocks.note: to have someone is to con them, a scam
a mine is a pit, losing T

explanation.surface: Ordering a shellfish dish in a restaurant with no time to spare.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Have mine' reads as ordering food, but 'have' means deceive, as in 'you've been had'; PIT loses its T.
explanation.definitionFit: Scampi are langoustines, usually served breaded and fried, a popular British pub shellfish dish.

clue.text: Philosophical sort almost shut in thus

indicators.note: being in something means sitting inside it, so one piece is enclosed by another

blocks.note: sic is Latin for thus
a door pulled to is closed or nearly so

explanation.surface: A thoughtful person nearly confined in this way.
explanation.walkthrough: A door that is 'to' is pushed nearly or fully closed; sic is the Latin word used in quotations to mean 'thus'.
explanation.definitionFit: A Stoic follows the school of Zeno, and more loosely is anyone who bears hardship calmly, philosophically.

clue.text: Greeks initially beat back bloodsucker

indicators.note: initially means at the start, so only the opening letter is kept
going back runs the letters in the opposite direction

blocks.note: first letter
to tan someone's hide is to beat them

explanation.surface: Greek warriors driving back a vampire.
explanation.walkthrough: To tan is informal for to thrash.
explanation.definitionFit: Female gnats bite and feed on blood, so the small fly is a bloodsucking insect.

clue.text: Good drive coming to nothing — call for old player

blocks.note: G is the abbreviation for good
to ram is to drive forcefully
O is zero, nothing
to phone someone is to call them

explanation.surface: A veteran sportsman's fine shot comes to nothing and someone shouts for him.
explanation.walkthrough: Drive and player suggest golf or cricket, but the player plays records.
explanation.definitionFit: A gramophone is the early wind-up machine for playing records, an antique device for reproducing recorded sound.

clue.text: Accountant trained recalled scholastic life

indicators.note: something recalled is called back, so its letters run the other way

blocks.note: ACA is an Associate of the Institute of Chartered Accountants
to train a gun is to aim it

explanation.surface: A qualified bookkeeper looks back on student days.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Trained' suggests professional training, but it means pointed, as a weapon is trained on a target.
explanation.definitionFit: Academia is the world of universities, research and learning, the community and environment of scholars.

clue.text: Partly processed food to become solid in batter?

blocks.note: cud is food a cow has partly digested and brings back up to chew
to gel is to set or become solid

explanation.surface: Kitchen talk of a semi-prepared ingredient setting in pancake mix.
explanation.walkthrough: Batter suggests cooking, with the question mark flagging that it is really the verb to beat.
explanation.definitionFit: To cudgel someone is to hit them repeatedly with a short thick club, a way to pound or beat.
